authorship: Agewise authored conditional strategic guidance, not a pro quotation or a validated combat model
patch_policy: Strategy is conditional. Catalog availability, bonuses and base values retain their separately pinned patch; none establishes actual forces or affordability.

mechanics_reference.facts: Hash-verified catalog costs, times, namespaced entities, civilization availability and descriptions only.
mechanics_reference.strategy: The principles and conditional interactions are authored interpretations, not externally sourced professional verdicts. External strategic-quality review remains pending.

concepts.title: Commit, regroup, or disengage?
concepts.summary: A tactical order was followed by a move or stop input to overlapping selected IDs. This is a commitment-change checkpoint, not proof of a battle or retreat.
concepts.principle: Fight only while the actual local numbers, upgrades, terrain and support justify it. A nominal counter can still lose; preserve valuable units and use mobility or reinforcement when the exchange becomes unfavorable.
concepts.practice: Before committing, name your local advantage and one disengagement route. Reassess when support or numbers change, rather than following the first order automatically.
concepts.question: Was the follow-up a planned maneuver, a successful raid, or a response to unfavorable contact? Would waiting for reinforcements, changing position or avoiding the fight have preserved useful forces?
concepts.hypothesis: The command sequence identifies a decision change; it cannot establish who was present, who won or whether movement completed.
concepts.exception: A move after an attack order may be a successful maneuver, scouting or an accidental input; retreat is not automatically correct.
required_state_for_verdict: actual opposing compositions and local numbers

options.if: Your local force and support cannot take a favorable exchange.
options.then: Disengage toward support, reinforce or choose a different position; protect high-value units.
options.not_claimed: That this was a losing engagement or that a safe route existed.

options.if: You have a real local advantage and a useful objective.
options.then: Commit with support and a reinforcement route, reassessing when the advantage changes.
options.not_claimed: That a counter label or civ bonus guarantees victory.

concepts.title: Balance expansion with army replacement
concepts.summary: An economic expansion or efficiency input overlaps military production requests. Review which investment could become useful before the next military demand.
concepts.principle: Maintain enough economy to fund the plan, but turn that economy into fielded replacements before adding expansion that cannot help the immediate situation. There is no universal villager cap.
concepts.practice: Before the next expansion investment, check the army you can field, surviving production and the next replacement wave. Allocate resources to the immediate bottleneck, not a fixed villager target.
concepts.question: Could existing forces hold while the economy investment paid back, or did replacements, population room, resources or safe reinforcement routes deserve priority?
concepts.hypothesis: Simultaneous economy and army inputs create an allocation question, not evidence of an oversized economy, army losses or unused capacity.
concepts.exception: Expansion may be a sensible recovery or a safe long-term investment; military requests can already be adequately supported.

options.if: The current army cannot hold and replacement production is feasible.
options.then: Fund the replacement wave or reallocate workers/resources before more economic expansion.
options.not_claimed: That army losses, overbooming or production idle time were measured.

options.if: Existing defense buys time and economic payback serves the plan.
options.then: Continue expansion while preserving military replacement and population capacity.
options.not_claimed: That the map was safe or a particular villager count was optimal.

concepts.title: Make extra production solve a bottleneck
concepts.summary: Separate military-building placement inputs occur alongside military queue requests. Check what the extra capacity was intended to accomplish.
concepts.principle: Add production when it supports a feasible composition or reinforcement need. If resources, population, upgrades or route safety are the bottleneck, more buildings alone may not help.
concepts.practice: Before adding the next military building, name the unit, the required replacement rate and the resources/population that will keep it useful. Adapt if another bottleneck is limiting the army.
concepts.question: Were the placements replacement infrastructure, a composition transition, useful capacity, or investment ahead of demand? Which bottleneck should the next resources address?
concepts.hypothesis: Placement and queue inputs support a capacity-investment question, not a count of surviving or unnecessary buildings.
concepts.exception: Replacing destroyed production, shortening reinforcement routes or transitioning composition may justify additional buildings.

options.if: Existing capacity is funded and insufficient for the required army.
options.then: Add suitable capacity where reinforcements can reach the objective safely.
options.not_claimed: That the existing buildings were saturated or survived.

options.if: Resources, population or an unsuitable composition limit useful output.
options.then: Fix that constraint before adding another production building.
options.not_claimed: That the new building was unnecessary merely because several placements were recorded.

concepts.title: Secure access before committing the position
concepts.summary: A resource-camp or fortification placement was requested away from the verified starting TC. Its value depends on access and the ability to support it, not just the placement.
concepts.principle: Contest territory that protects useful resources or reinforcement access. If the position cannot be supported, choose safer access or a deliberate withdrawal instead of paying repeatedly to defend an isolated investment.
concepts.practice: Before committing to a distant resource or fortification, identify its purpose, a support route and a fallback. Reassess access if enemy pressure changes the route.
concepts.question: Did this location secure needed resources or shorten reinforcements, or expose builders and future traffic? Which nearer resource, different approach or withdrawal was feasible?
concepts.hypothesis: Distance from the initial TC locates a requested investment; it does not establish current borders, resource ownership or enemy control.
concepts.exception: The starting TC is not the current base boundary; this may be a safe expansion, an already defended site or a useful forward position.
required_state_for_verdict: actual map control and player vision

options.if: The position secures useful access and can be protected.
options.then: Support it with a safe reinforcement route and a fallback rather than treating construction as control.
options.not_claimed: That the placement completed or the territory was controlled.

options.if: Builders or reinforcements would be isolated.
options.then: Use a safer resource or approach, regroup, or withdraw before committing more resources.
options.not_claimed: That another resource or route was actually open.

concepts.title: Wall with a purpose and a follow-up
concepts.summary: A wall or gate placement input was recorded. Review the intended route closure, access and follow-up rather than assuming the base became safe.
concepts.principle: Use feasible small walls, chokes or a fallback to protect useful work. Preserve exits and reinforcement access; walls buy options only if completed, closed and supported against the actual threat.
concepts.practice: For the next defensive wall, name the approach it blocks, check the actual gap and an exit, then choose the army or fallback that makes the wall useful.
concepts.question: Was this a useful short closure or a planned layout? Did it leave a gap, isolate units or consume resources better used for a different defense?
concepts.hypothesis: A placement is an inspectable defensive-layout decision, not proof of a complete wall or a threat.
concepts.exception: An open map or mobile army may favor selective walls and active defense instead of full enclosure.
required_state_for_verdict: completed wall segments, gates and gaps

options.if: A short closure protects exposed work and is feasible.
options.then: Complete the relevant gap, keep an exit and provide an appropriate defensive follow-up.
options.not_claimed: That the recorded wall completed or held.

options.if: A full enclosure blocks your own plan or cannot hold the threat.
options.then: Use a choke, selective wall, repositioning or active defense instead.
options.not_claimed: That always walling or never walling is correct.

concepts.title: Match upgrades to the army you can field
concepts.summary: An army-upgrade request appears with related unit-queue inputs. Review the investment's timing and the force that could use it.
concepts.principle: Choose upgrades and transitions for a feasible composition and the next decision. An upgrade request is not completion, and a correct counter still needs numbers, support and positioning.
concepts.practice: Before the next army upgrade, name the force it benefits, when it can matter and what production or defense must continue while it is researched.
concepts.question: Did this upgrade reinforce a usable army, prepare a transition, or compete with urgent replacements? Was scouting sufficient to justify the composition?
concepts.hypothesis: Related research and production inputs describe investment intent, not upgraded units or a successful counter.
concepts.exception: A forward-looking upgrade or defensive adaptation may be sensible even before a large army exists.

options.if: A usable force and the next objective benefit from the upgrade in time.
options.then: Support the upgrade with continued production, protection and a feasible transition.
options.not_claimed: That the research completed or the bonus was active.

options.if: Immediate survival or replacements cannot wait for the investment.
options.then: Consider fieldable units or a defensive adaptation before the longer-term upgrade.
options.not_claimed: That the upgrade was a mistake or the counter would win automatically.
